transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-04
Start time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 54 minutes
Attendees: Evan Clarke (Redwood AE), Maya Rao (Redwood SE), Jordan Lee (Voyager CTO), Priya Singh (Voyager Infra), Marco Ruiz (Voyager Security)

Summary:
Brief discovery focused on Voyager's requirements for a Private/VPC deployment of Redwood. Discussion covered networking (VPC peering vs Transit Gateway), private endpoints (interface endpoints/PrivateLink), CIDR and overlapping ranges, region constraints for data residency, KMS integration and audit logs, and next steps for architecture runbook and a technical deep-dive.

Topics:
- Private VPC deployment options and high level network topology
- VPC peering vs Transit Gateway / TGW considerations
- PrivateLink / interface endpoints, S3 endpoint access, ECR/EKS implications
- Region/AZ constraints and data residency
- Security: KMS, HSM, SOC2, audit logs, SAML/Okta SSO
- Pilot plan and basic timeline

Action items (brief): see metadata above.

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Evan Clarke: Hey everyone thanks for joining, uh this is Evan with Redwood, I am the AE on this account, joining me is Maya our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:00:08] Jordan Lee: Good thanks, Jordan here. We've got Priya and Marco on the line too. Thanks for making time.
[00:00:13] Priya Singh: Hi all.
[00:00:15] Marco Ruiz: Hey.
[00:00:18] Maya Rao: Great, quick agenda — we'll do a 10 minute intro to Redwood's Private offering, then dig into your networking constraints and compliance, and finish with next steps. Sound good?
[00:00:27] Jordan Lee: Yep that's perfect. We're primarily evaluating Private so we can keep inference inside our VPCs and satisfy some regulatory things for EU customer data.
[00:00:36] Evan Clarke: Totally makes sense. To set context, Redwood Private runs a customer-controlled control plane — either VPC peering or interface endpoints are both supported depending on your preference. Maya, do you want to start with the topology options?
[00:00:46] Maya Rao: Sure. There are a couple common patterns we see. One is VPC peering from your VPCs to Redwood-managed VPCs in the same region, another is using AWS Transit Gateway for centralized routing if you have many VPCs, and the third is PrivateLink / interface endpoints so our service becomes an interface endpoint in your VPC. Each has pros/cons around egress cost, route table complexity and cross-account permissions.
[00:01:06] Priya Singh: Quick question — our infra team prefers Transit Gateway because we have 40+ VPCs across accounts, peering that many is messy. Is TGW fully supported?
[00:01:15] Maya Rao: Yes, TGW is supported. We can attach Redwood's VPCs to your TGW and we coordinate the routing with your network team. One caveat: with TGW you need to ensure the correct route propagation and avoid overlapping CIDRs — that tends to be the most common friction.
[00:01:29] Jordan Lee: About CIDR ranges — our primary account uses 10.0.0.0/16 and we have several subnets. We also have a legacy on-prem VPN with 192.168.0.0/16. Will that cause issues?
[00:01:39] Maya Rao: Overlap with Redwood's VPCs is something we check for. We typically recommend providing us with the exact CIDR blocks so we avoid conflicts. If there's overlap we can either change the Redwood VPC allocation or use interface endpoints which avoids cross-VPC routing but uses PrivateLink.
[00:01:52] Marco Ruiz: And from a security perspective, we need to minimize egress to the public internet. If we use peering or TGW, do requests to model servers go over the private path only?
[00:02:01] Evan Clarke: Yes, the idea is private connectivity. With VPC peering or TGW the traffic stays on AWS network. With PrivateLink/interface endpoints, the data path never traverses public internet either. However you should consider whether you want outbound access to S3 or ECR — we support endpoint policies and S3 interface/gateway endpoints for S3 access.
[00:02:19] Priya Singh: Ok. How about regional availability — we need eu-west-1 and us-east-1 for redundancy and to satisfy data residency. Do you have presence in those regions?
[00:02:28] Maya Rao: We have Redwood Private availability in eu-west-1 and us-east-1. For the pilot we can stand up in eu-west-1 for EU data residency and optionally mirror logs/metrics to us-east-1 if you want cross-region failover. We typically recommend keeping inference serving in-region for latency reasons.
[00:02:41] Jordan Lee: Latency's important — our SLAs are 200ms P95. For some edge cases we might accept higher but ideally we need sub-200ms for chat-like features. How do you validate that in Private?
[00:02:52] Maya Rao: We run benchmarks using your representative prompt set. For in-region deployments on GPU-backed nodes our typical P95 is under 150ms for shorter prompts but it depends on model size and token budget. For strict SLAs we can propose dedicated capacity (Redwood Dedicated) where capacity is reserved which yields more predictable latency.
[00:03:06] Priya Singh: Dedicated is interesting — but does that change the network setup?
[00:03:09] Evan Clarke: Not really from a customer perspective. Dedicated is more about reserved GPU pools and capacity isolation; networking still follows the Private deployment patterns — TGW, peering, or PrivateLink.
[00:03:21] Marco Ruiz: On the security side, questions about KMS — we require that the key material remains under our control. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS/HSM?
[00:03:28] Maya Rao: Yes, Redwood Private supports customer-managed KMS for encrypting persisted artifacts. For key operations we can integrate with your AWS KMS or bring-your-own HSM in on-prem setups. We'll share the KMS integration doc.
[00:03:39] Marco Ruiz: Great. Also we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM and retention of request-level audit trails for 12 months.
[00:03:45] Evan Clarke: We can forward audit logs to your CloudWatch or S3 bucket over a private endpoint and integrate with your SIEM. Retention policies we can configure; longer retention is an add-on if needed.
[00:03:55] Priya Singh: One practical item — egress NAT/Gateway. If we route traffic via TGW back to your subnets, do we need NAT for the model servers to pull model artifacts from S3?
[00:04:04] Maya Rao: Good callout. For initial image/artifact pulls we can pull from S3 via VPC endpoint so you don't need NAT for that. Ongoing inference traffic doesn't require outbound internet unless you want to send metrics or connect to external APIs. We can set up endpoint policies for ECR, S3, and KMS.
[00:04:19] Jordan Lee: What about DNS — do you set up private hosted zones for service discovery or do we manage that?
[00:04:24] Maya Rao: We typically create interface endpoints which provide private DNS entries in your account. If you prefer, we can use your private hosted zone and manage records, but most customers let the interface endpoints handle DNS automatically.
[00:04:36] Marco Ruiz: Any compliance paperwork you can share? SOC2, pen test reports, that kind of thing.
[00:04:41] Evan Clarke: Yes we'll send the SOC2 report and our security whitepaper. We also have a short compliance checklist that maps to common requirements. I'll attach those in the follow-up.
[00:04:49] Priya Singh: Network ports — do you require specific inbound ports in our NACLs or security groups?
[00:04:54] Maya Rao: We mostly use HTTPS over 443 for control plane and TLS for model traffic. For private connectivity the traffic is internal, but you'll need to allow the relevant CIDR ranges in your security groups. We'll provide the minimal set.
[00:05:06] Jordan Lee: If we go with PrivateLink — are there extra charges?
[00:05:10] Evan Clarke: Yes there's AWS charges for interface endpoints and data processing on PrivateLink; those show up on your bill. We can estimate costs based on expected throughput and model token rates. That's part of the cost analysis we provide during pilot planning.
[00:05:22] Priya Singh: OK, we also have a requirement around regional peering — our EU accounts are in eu-west-1 and we cannot route EU customer data out of region. So the inference must occur entirely in eu-west-1. Can Redwood guarantee that?
[00:05:33] Maya Rao: Yes we can pin deployments to specific regions and ensure data doesn't egress. For multi-region we can set up per-region deployments and a routing policy. The control plane can be localized too in Private so you don't have control-plane egress. We'll need to validate the exact data flows in the architecture doc.
[00:05:47] Marco Ruiz: One more security question — SSO integrations: we use Okta and SCIM for provisioning. Does Redwood support SAML/SCIM and role-based access?
[00:05:54] Evan Clarke: Yes SAML SSO and SCIM provisioning are supported, plus fine-grained RBAC for console and API keys. We'll include the SSO integration guide in the follow-up.
[00:06:02] Jordan Lee: Great. Priya — any additional infra details you want to call out?
[00:06:06] Priya Singh: We run EKS across accounts, our CI pulls images from a private ECR. For model artifacts we'd prefer they live in our ECR or an S3 bucket in the same account, not Redwood-managed buckets if possible.
[00:06:17] Maya Rao: We can pull from your ECR (with cross-account roles) or have you provide S3 access via VPC endpoints. If you want Redwood to push logs or model outputs to your bucket, we'll use an IAM role and you keep control of the bucket.
[00:06:28] Jordan Lee: Sounds good. What's the recommended pilot scope?
[00:06:31] Evan Clarke: Pilot scope typically is: one region (eu-west-1), one VPC connection method (TGW or interface endpoint), a small dedicated pool for predictable latency, and run a 72-hour benchmark with your prompt set. We then review metrics and tweak sizing.
[00:06:45] Marco Ruiz: Can the benchmark include audit log verification and SIEM forwarding?
[00:06:48] Maya Rao: Yes we can include log forwarding and retention checks as part of the pilot acceptance criteria.
[00:06:53] Jordan Lee: Timeline-wise, if we get the CIDR ranges and confirm region, how quickly can we stand up a pilot?
[00:06:58] Evan Clarke: Once we have CIDRs and an agreed topology, typical lead time is 5-7 business days to provision the Private stack and coordinate access. If we need hardware or dedicated capacity it could be a bit longer.
[00:07:09] Priya Singh: Ok we'll aim to share details by Monday.
[00:07:12] Evan Clarke: Great. Quick wrap — I'll send the VPC architecture diagram, SOC2 and KMS docs, and a proposed pilot plan. Maya will reach out to schedule the technical deep-dive with your infra team. Anything else?
[00:07:23] Jordan Lee: No that's it from me, thanks folks.
[00:07:26] Marco Ruiz: Thanks.
[00:07:27] Priya Singh: Thanks, bye.
[00:07:30] Evan Clarke: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with those artifacts. Bye.
